title: Поздний банкет для официанток  (A Late Banquet for the Waitresses)

segments.t: At the end of the night, Chef Barinov dismisses the exhausted kitchen crew, only for a waitress to announce that Vika has seated a party of eight VIP guests. After the cooks stay late to prepare the feast, Viktor Petrovich walks into the dining room and finds Vika and the waitresses eating it themselves.
Ещё заказы, пришла компания из восьми человек.
Ну что ж, спасибо вам за поздний ужин.
Let's replay the exchange and look closely at each Russian phrase.

'Alright, single-celled organisms.' Barinov jumps in boldly right here and reaches for the Russian word "odnokletochnyye" ("single-celled", built from "odnokletochnyy") right at the center of the line.
'Everyone is dismissed, see you tomorrow.' Insisting on how free things are at once, Vika links the Russian words directly in the present with no word for "am", "is", or "are" needed.
'Bye, everyone.' Barinov gently delivers this casual farewell in one quick breath using "poka" ("bye") — the quick everyday word for "bye for now" between people on close terms.
Ещё заказы, пришла компания из восьми человек.
'More orders just came in, a party of eight arrived.' Addressing the company right here, Vika uses "kompaniya" ("the company") to carry the main weight of the thought.
'What more orders? It is time to go home.' Discussing the orders on the spot, Barinov leans on "pora" ("it is time to"), which carries the whole predicate in Russian without needing "it is".
'It is time to go home.' Vika speaks up lightly toward Barinov, shifting the mood of the conversation in a single beat.
'But Viktoriya Sergeyevna said.' Turning candidly to Vika, spoken Russian compresses the whole thought into just 4 words, skipping the extra helper words English needs.
'That these are very important guests.' Showing how important things are to Barinov, Vika links the Russian words directly in the present with no word for "am", "is", or "are" needed.
'Well, just make it quick.' Barinov continues lightly without holding back, keeping the focus on what actually matters here.
'Everything tastes so delicious.' Vika speaks up pointedly right here and puts the weight on "vkusnenko" ("deliciously", from "vkusno") as the exchange unfolds.
Ну что ж, спасибо вам за поздний ужин.
'Well then, thank you so much for the late dinner.' Barinov chimes in calmly without holding back, bringing things back to earth after the buildup.
'Wait, I do not get it.' Vika continues promptly toward Barinov, shifting the mood of the conversation in a single beat.

'Thanks a lot, guys.' Barinov plainly directs this word of thanks in the exchange using "spasibo" ("thank you") — the everyday word for "thank you", which grew out of the old blessing "spasi Bog" ("God save you").
Ещё заказы, пришла компания из восьми человек.
Ну что ж, спасибо вам за поздний ужин.

That wraps up this scene as just as the cooks are packing up to go home, Vika orders the kitchen to prepare a late dinner for eight VIP guests—who turn out to be Vika and her waitresses. See you next time!

Ну что ж, спасибо вам за поздний ужин
